name: Daria Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm unit manager at Westmoor Pigs. Four hundred sows, so about nine thousand pigs a year going through, plus two hundred hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes into our own feed. I'm in at half six, read the overnight data on my phone, then walk the farrowing house, that's where sows give birth. We've got microphones that listen for coughing and flag a pen before I can hear it. I love farrowing, the new litters. What wears me out is the smell in your hair and the hours at weaning time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to check feed conversion, plan the weaning batches, and write up the vet reports. I'd use it more if the owners let me. I live with Tom, he's an electrician, in a rented cottage near Westmoor. We go to St Mary's on Sundays. We've got about five months saved, and the plan is our own small farm one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. That would be a disappointment, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use the tools, they're useful, but don't wait for a miracle. Hard work and good stockmanship still win. I'd probably post our cough-monitor results on the pig forum anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit let down. I want the tech to take the dull work so I can focus on the animals and on building something of my own. In this picture I just keep grafting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep saving for our own place, maybe a small pig and arable unit to rent. I'd push the owners to try the robot washer for the pens, because washing out is the worst job and nobody stays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own place look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty sows, outdoor, and some barley. Small enough that Tom and I could run it with one helper. We'd sell some pork direct. It's a long way off, but it's the dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it never happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody but us, mostly. Land's dear, the banks are cautious. But that's the market. I'd just have to work harder or wait longer.

S0.say: I'd say use the tools because they're useful, but don't wait for a miracle, because hard work and good stockmanship still win. She'd still post her cough-monitor results on a pig forum.
S0.think: Privately she'd be a bit let down, having hoped the technology would take the dull work. She'd just keep grafting toward a farm of her own.
S0.do: Carries on as unit manager while saving for a small rented pig and arable unit. Pushes the owners to try a pen-washing robot for the job nobody wants.
S0.quote: I want the tech to take the dull work so I can focus on the animals and on building something of my own.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is ambitious and comfortable with technology, but her goal is old-fashioned: her own family farm. She takes personal responsibility rather than blaming anyone. A stalled AI future slows her plans but doesn't change them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's exciting. That's the one I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farming, if farmers own the machines. I'd tell young people to learn it, not fear it. I'd say it at the young farmers' club, to the pig forum, at church if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think people like me win in this picture. I already run the data side. The farm needs fewer hands but someone who can manage the systems, and that's me. The risk is the big pig companies getting cheaper still and squeezing small units like the one I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the case to the owners for automated feeding and the pen washer, with numbers. I'd ask for a bonus tied to results. And I'd start looking seriously for a small unit to rent, because if the kit gets cheaper, a small farm with robots could run with two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly excited. It's like a good harvest coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out on the farm if you brought in the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin, who does the washing out, and maybe one of the stockmen. I'd feel bad. I'd want them moved to other work if there was any. But I'd still do it, because if we don't, the farm down the road will and we'll all be out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if farmers own the machines'. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean not renting everything from a tech company that can switch it off. If I buy the robot, it's mine. Like a tractor. I don't want to be a tenant on my own farm.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for farming if farmers own the machines, and tell young people to learn it rather than fear it. She'd say it at the young farmers' club and on the pig forum.
S1.think: Privately she thinks people like her win, since farms need fewer hands but someone to run the systems. The risk is big pig companies squeezing small units like the one she wants.
S1.do: Makes a numbers-based case for automated feeding and a pen washer and asks for a results-linked bonus. Starts looking seriously for a small unit to rent, run by two people with robots.
S1.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited, like a good harvest coming in.
S1.quote: I don't want to be a tenant on my own farm.
S1.fieldNote: Her line on owning the machines blends free-market thinking with a strong sense of independence. She admits the cost to two colleagues and goes ahead anyway, reasoning that competitors would. She sees automation as the route to her own farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's fast. Even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, get practical, and look after your family and your church. I wouldn't want the government taking over farming because of it. People should be free to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me more than I'd say. If AI runs the whole pig unit, the owners don't need a manager. And if big firms can run robot farms cheap, my small farm dream doesn't add up. Two years is too fast to buy in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd look for a small unit to rent before prices move, and I'd use most of our savings as a deposit on kit. Tom could do the electrics. I'd keep my job as long as they'd have me. I'd sell pork direct from day one, so we're not at the mercy of the big buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Restless and wired, like before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting most of your savings into a farm in that picture. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But sitting still is a risk too. If the whole job market goes, I'd rather own something real, land and animals, than have five months in the bank. Money in the bank doesn't feed you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have to take my big chance now, before I'm ready. With more time I'd save more and pick the right farm. With two years I'd take whatever came up.

S2.say: I'd say don't panic, get practical and look after your family and church. She'd say the government shouldn't take over farming and people should be free to adapt.
S2.think: Privately it scares her more than she'd admit, since an AI-run unit doesn't need a manager. Cheap robot farms might also make her small-farm dream stop adding up.
S2.do: Rushes to rent a small unit before prices move and puts most of the savings into kit, with her partner doing the electrics. Keeps her job as long as possible and sells pork direct from the start.
S2.feel: Anxious and wired, like before an exam.
S2.quote: Money in the bank doesn't feed you.
S2.fieldNote: Her reaction to the fast picture is to make her move early and own something real. She plays down fear in public and admits it in private. She clearly rejects relying on government, even under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's my window, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for young farmers who are ready to work and learn. Don't wait for handouts, get skills, get ready. I'd probably run a session at the young farmers' club on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to save more, find the right farm, and set it up with robots before the big firms swallow everything. It's tight but it's doable. I think in five years I could have my own pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, save hard, up to eight months. Year two, rent a small unit, fifty sows outdoors. Buy secondhand automation as the bigger farms upgrade. Use AI for the books, the breeding plan, the direct sales. And Tom and I would get married in year one, because we'd be signing for a farm together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Like I can see the gate I'm aiming for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said get married because you'd be signing together. Is that the only reason?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. No. We've been meaning to for two years. But yes, this would hurry it up. My mum would be delighted. Father Peter would be delighted. Tom would pretend he's not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum and dad. They're not farmers, they work in a shop and a care home. Those jobs might go too, and they've not got much saved. I'd want room for them on the farm if it came to it.

S3.say: I'd say this is a chance for young farmers ready to work and learn, so get skills and don't wait for handouts. She'd likely run a session on it at the young farmers' club.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is enough to save more, find the right farm and set it up with robots before big firms take everything. It's tight but doable.
S3.do: Saves toward eight months in year one, then rents a small outdoor unit of about fifty sows in year two, buying secondhand automation. Uses AI for the books and sales and marries her partner in year one.
S3.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, like seeing the gate she's aiming for.
S3.quote: I think in five years I could have my own pigs.
S3.fieldNote: She sees five years as her ideal window and lays out a clear, year-by-year plan. Family runs through it: the wedding and room on the farm for her parents. Her outlook is self-reliance, but family is her safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty of time. Maybe too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Learn the tools, save, and build something that's yours. I'd be encouraging, not preachy, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the risk with ten years is everyone else gets ready too. The big firms would buy up land, and young farmers would be fighting over the same small units. My edge shrinks. But it's safer, so I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Westmoor a few more years, learning every new system. Save to a year's worth. Around year four, rent or buy a small unit and start with thirty sows. Marry Tom, start a family, and build the direct sales slowly. Get the kids feeding piglets as soon as they can walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really. That one sounds like a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd gamble everything. Ten years, I can plan it like a proper business. Five is my favourite, honestly, it's just right. But ten would be the safest for a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about kids on the farm. What if robots do all the work by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'd learn to run the robots and still know how to hold a piglet. I'd want them to know both. Faith, family and knowing your animals. Machines don't change that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it to learn the tools, save and build something of your own. She hopes she'd sound encouraging, not preachy.
S4.think: Privately she thinks ten years lets everyone get ready, so big firms buy land and young farmers fight over small units. Her edge shrinks, but it's safer.
S4.do: Stays in her job a few more years learning each new system and saves toward a year's worth of expenses. Around year four rents or buys a small unit with thirty sows, marries, starts a family and builds direct sales.
S4.feel: Calm and happy, because it sounds like a life.
S4.quote: Then they'd learn to run the robots and still know how to hold a piglet.
S4.fieldNote: She weighs timelines like a business but picks the slow one as best for a family. More warning means more competition for her, a view she shares with other quick adopters. Her picture of the future blends robots with faith and family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have to bet everything before I'm ready, and if it went wrong, Tom and I would have nothing. What would help is easier ways for young farmers to rent or buy small units, like starter farms from councils and fair loans, not grants with strings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pigs. People think pig farming is cruel and a robot farm would be worse. I don't. I think a good farmer with good machines would treat them better. But that depends on the farmer.

headlineQuote: I don't want to be a tenant on my own farm.
portrait: Daria Dubois is a 27-year-old unit manager at a 400-sow pig farm with its own feed crops, who uses AI every day to manage data, breeding and reports. She lives with her partner Tom, an electrician, goes to church on Sundays and has about five months saved toward a farm of their own. She's traditional and free-market, dislikes handouts and wants farmers to own their machines rather than rent them from tech firms. She sees every picture as a chance to get her own pigs, and calls five years her ideal window. In the fast picture she'd stake her savings early, while ten years means more competition but a safer path for a family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have to bet everything on a farm before she's ready and could lose it all.
whatWouldHelp: Easier ways for young farmers to rent or buy small units, such as council starter farms and fair loans rather than grants with strings.
